what: What the dataset asserts, what its own scripts compare it against, and — since 2026-09-16 — what the paper beside it prints. The record (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.18408002, 2026-01-29) shipped with no paper (the scripts cite 'Waves breaking similarity at natural sea?, submitted to GRL, 2021' with no DOI); the paper appeared in Geophysical Research Letters on 2026-09-16 and its printed numbers are transcribed under `paper`. Nothing in this file is computed here.
description: Breaking wave geometry has historically been investigated through laboratory studies, with very limited open ocean observations. Understanding wave geometry is key for modeling air-sea gas exchange, energy dissipation, and satellite measurements. We measured the geometry—including area, length, height, duration, and speed—of over 16000 breaking waves in the Black Sea. Our analysis reveals that real-world breaking waves do not conform to a self-similar geometry, nor are there predictable relationships between a wave's breaking speed and its geometric properties. The results indicate that wave breaking geometry is complex and sea-state dependent.

sentences.selfSimilar: real-world breaking waves do not conform to a self-similar geometry
sentences.speedGeometry: nor are there predictable relationships between a wave's breaking speed and its geometric properties
sentences.count: over 16000 breaking waves in the Black Sea

table.how: the per-event table the scripts read from blacksea_data.pkl (a pandas DataFrame pickle), written out with every double as the shortest decimal that round-trips to it (Python repr) and verified column by column against the pickle with a correctly-rounded parser; the literal in the CSV IS the double the record holds

columns.Rec: the stereo-video record (20 records, Black Sea, 2013-09-22 to 2013-10-02, 10–15 Hz)
columns.ev: the event index within the record
columns.DT: breaking duration, s (multiples of the frame interval)
columns.cm: mean breaking speed over the event, m/s (the scripts' c_b)
columns.Ab_max: largest plan-view area of the aerated region during the event, m²
columns.Pb_max: largest perimeter of the aerated region, m — the scripts take Lb = Pb_max/2 as the breaking length
columns.LD81: the slanted length √(Dz² + B²) at the frame of largest minor axis B: the scripts' Duncan (1981) length
columns.Dz_max: largest vertical extent of the aerated region, m
columns.theta: arctan(Dz / LD81) at that frame, degrees: the scripts' Duncan (1981) inclination
columns.sv_fp: peak frequency of the wave spectrum of the record, Hz (constant within a record)
columns.wnd: wind speed of the record, m/s (constant within a record)
columns.Hs: a column NAMED Hs, constant within a record, 0.20–0.75, every value a multiple of 1/256 — it is NOT the Hs the paper prints for the record (see paper.table1 and the ledger's columnIdentity)
columns.sv_fp2: constant within a record, 0.35–1.88: to two decimals it is the Hs column of the paper's Table 1 in every one of the 20 records (decided in the ledger); the name is the pickle's
columns.svA: reconstructed area of the record, m² (Table 1's area column)
columns.svT: duration of the record, s (Table 1's duration in minutes)
columns.LA_max: largest major axis of the enclosing ellipse, m — the paper's e_A (across-wave)
columns.LB_max: largest minor axis of the enclosing ellipse, m — the paper's e_B (along-wave)
columns.Ae_max: largest area of the enclosing ellipse, m²
columns.cA: mean speed component along the major axis, m/s
columns.cB: mean speed component along the minor axis, m/s — the paper's c_e

Lb.note: test_self_similarity.py and plot_linear_relation.py: 05Pr_max = Pb_max/2 is the breaking length L_b

duncanAngle.note: plot_histograms.py draws axvspan(10, 14.7, label='Duncan (1981)') on the histogram of theta; Duncan 1981 (Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 377, 331–348) is not held here, and the band is taken as the scripts state it

duncanAspect.note: plot_histograms.py draws axvline(0.11, label='Duncan (1981)') on the histogram of Ab_max / LD81²; Duncan's ratio relates the CROSS-SECTIONAL area of the breaking region to its length, while Ab here is a plan-view area — the comparison is the scripts' own, and is decided here as they drew it

selfSimilarity.note: test_self_similarity.py: three dimensionless ratios that a self-similar geometry would hold constant; the script marks the tail beyond mean + 2σ

speedGeometry.note: plot_linear_relation.py fits Lb = a·cb and Lb = a·cb²/g by RANSAC and least squares (float; not reproduced); the decided quantity here is the rank correlation, an exact rational

geometryGeometry.note: the same statistic between geometric properties, as the control the speed–geometry numbers are read against

cmOverCp.definition: cm / cp with cp = g / (2π · sv_fp)
cmOverCp.note: plot_histograms.py, panel (f): the breaking speed as a fraction of the peak phase speed; needs π, so it is enclosed

fitLb.form: Lb = a · cb²/g, g = 9.81, least squares through the origin (curve_fit on objective a·x²/9.81, plot_linear_relation.py)

pearsonSpeedMax.form: Pearson r < 0.45 for every speed–geometry pair, for cm, c0 and the e_B component

rDzEB.where: §3: r(Δzb_max, eB_max) = 0.7 — eB the minor ellipse axis (LB_max)

fitAbLD81.form: Ab = k · L_D81², through the origin

fitAbLb.form: Ab = k · Lb², through the origin

fitEAEB.form: eA = k · eB through the origin; r Pearson

fitAeAb.form: Ae = k · Ab through the origin

selfSimilarFraction.form: events with a ratio ≥ mean + 2·sd (sample sd, test_self_similarity.py: STD = 2, pandas .std()), per ratio; the ± is the spread across the three ratios and the sea states

fitLbTail.form: on the self-similar subset: Lb = a·cb², a·g printed; r = Pearson(cb², Lb) (stats.linregress(x_sim**2, y_sim))

fitLbRest.form: on the remaining events: the same fit and r

seaStateDependence.claim: geometric scaling is not constant but varies with the sea state
